words_in_context.p: The new bus route has been ______ for commuters on the east side of town. Trips that once took an hour now take twenty minutes, and riders no longer have to change buses.
w: confusing
unnoticed
expensive
words_in_context.e: Shorter trips and no transfers are benefits, so “helpful” fits. The other choices describe problems or a lack of impact that the text doesn’t support.

words_in_context.p: Sea otters are known for their ______ fur. With up to a million hairs per square inch, it is the densest coat of any mammal and keeps them warm in icy water.
w: bright
loose
rough
words_in_context.e: “Densest coat” with a million hairs per square inch means the fur is thick. Nothing in the text mentions color, looseness, or texture.

words_in_context.p: Maya Lin was only twenty-one when her design for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial was chosen. Although she was still a student, the judges ______ her plan over more than a thousand other entries.
w: ignored
copied
questioned
words_in_context.e: Her design “was chosen,” so the judges selected it. “Ignored” and “questioned” contradict that, and nothing suggests copying.

words_in_context.p: The bakery’s owner decided to ______ her hours during the holidays. Instead of closing at five, the shop now stays open until nine to serve extra customers.
w: shorten
announce
forget
words_in_context.e: Moving closing time from five to nine lengthens the hours. “Announce” is possible in general, but the example shows the hours themselves growing.

words_in_context.p: Because the desert receives so little rain, its plants must be ______ with water. Many cacti store moisture in their stems and release it slowly over months.
w: wasteful
generous
bored
words_in_context.e: Storing water and releasing it slowly shows plants being careful with a scarce resource. “Wasteful” and “generous” say the opposite.

words_in_context.p: The two brothers had very ______ interests. One spent every weekend hiking in the mountains, while the other rarely left his apartment and preferred to paint.
w: similar
popular
secret
words_in_context.e: The sentence contrasts hiking outdoors with painting indoors, so their interests are different. “Similar” reverses that contrast.

words_in_context.p: Early reviewers dismissed Zora Neale Hurston’s novel for its use of Southern Black dialect, but later scholars have ______ that same feature, arguing that her ear for spoken language is what gives the book its lasting power.
w: overlooked
imitated
disputed
words_in_context.e: The word “but” sets later scholars against the early dismissal, and they say the feature gives the book its power, so they praised it. “Disputed” would agree with the critics, and “overlooked” conflicts with discussing it.

words_in_context.p: Engineers often describe concrete as a surprisingly ______ material. Although it resists enormous crushing forces, it cracks easily when stretched, which is why builders embed steel bars inside it to carry tension.
w: flexible
temporary
lightweight
words_in_context.e: Concrete is strong in one way and weak in another, so its performance is uneven. It cracks when stretched, which rules out “flexible,” and the text says nothing about weight or lifespan.

words_in_context.p: The historian’s account of the 1918 influenza outbreak is notably ______: rather than relying on government records alone, she draws on diaries, hospital ledgers, and letters from dozens of small towns.
w: brief
biased
outdated
words_in_context.e: The colon introduces a list of many kinds of sources, which shows thoroughness. Nothing suggests the account is short, slanted, or old.

words_in_context.p: Honeybees that find a rich patch of flowers do not keep the discovery to themselves. Returning to the hive, a forager performs a “waggle dance” that ______ the distance and direction of the food to her nestmates.
w: conceals
exaggerates
restricts
words_in_context.e: The first sentence says bees share what they find, so the dance communicates, or conveys, the location. “Conceals” is the opposite, and nothing suggests the information is inflated.

words_in_context.p: Critics of the proposed dam argue that its benefits have been ______. They note that the projected electricity output relies on rainfall figures from an unusually wet decade and is unlikely to be reached in a typical year.
w: misplaced
postponed
undisclosed
words_in_context.e: Output projections based on an unusually wet decade make the benefits look larger than they are: overstated. The benefits are publicly projected, so “undisclosed” doesn’t fit.

words_in_context.p: Though the composer’s late symphonies are now staples of the concert hall, audiences at their premieres were ______. Contemporary newspapers describe half-empty seats and polite, scattered applause rather than outrage or enthusiasm.
w: hostile
delighted
mistaken
words_in_context.e: Half-empty seats and polite applause, “rather than outrage or enthusiasm,” describe indifference. “Hostile” and “delighted” are the two reactions the text specifically rules out.

words_in_context.p: The biologist Lynn Margulis spent years defending the idea that complex cells arose when simpler organisms merged. Her colleagues initially treated the theory as eccentric, yet genetic evidence eventually proved so ______ that the claim, once a fringe position, now appears in standard textbooks.
w: ambiguous
fragmentary
conventional
words_in_context.e: Evidence that moved a fringe idea into textbooks must have been convincing, or compelling. “Ambiguous” and “fragmentary” would not have won over skeptics, and “conventional” describes the theory’s later status, not the evidence.

words_in_context.p: In her study of nineteenth-century factory towns, the economist does not claim that wages alone explain workers’ migration; she is careful to ______ her argument, noting that family ties, housing, and religious communities also shaped where people chose to settle.
w: abandon
reiterate
popularize
words_in_context.e: To qualify an argument is to limit it by adding conditions, which is what noting other factors does. She doesn’t give it up (“abandon”), and adding other factors is more than repeating it (“reiterate”).

words_in_context.p: Some philosophers of science warn against treating a successful theory as a final truth. History, they observe, is littered with models that predicted observations accurately for generations before being replaced. On this view, a theory’s present success is ______ evidence of its truth: encouraging, perhaps, but far from conclusive.
w: irrefutable
irrelevant
deceptive
words_in_context.e: “Encouraging, perhaps, but far from conclusive” means the evidence holds for now and could be revised: provisional. “Irrefutable” contradicts “far from conclusive,” and “irrelevant” and “deceptive” are too dismissive of “encouraging.”

words_in_context.p: Readers who come to Marianne Moore’s poems expecting grand emotional declarations may find them ______. Moore preferred precise observation to open confession, and her feeling tends to surface obliquely, through a carefully chosen detail about an animal or an object rather than a direct statement.
w: sentimental
chaotic
derivative
words_in_context.e: Poems that avoid open confession and let feeling surface only indirectly are reserved, or reticent. “Sentimental” is the opposite, and nothing suggests disorder or imitation.

words_in_context.p: The treaty’s drafters deliberately left several key terms undefined. Far from an oversight, this ______ allowed delegations with sharply opposed positions to sign the same document, each confident that it could later interpret the language in its own favor.
w: urgency
rigidity
secrecy
words_in_context.e: Undefined terms that each side can read its own way are examples of vagueness. “Rigidity” is the opposite, and nothing in the text concerns speed or keeping the terms hidden.

words_in_context.p: Archaeologists had long assumed that the settlement was abandoned suddenly after a catastrophe. New excavations ______ that assumption: layers of carefully sealed storerooms and the orderly removal of tools suggest residents departed gradually and may have expected to return.
w: corroborate
anticipate
exemplify
words_in_context.e: A gradual, planned departure conflicts with a sudden abandonment, so the evidence undermines the assumption. “Corroborate” and “exemplify” would mean the evidence supports it.

text_structure.s: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
text_structure.p: Many people think bats are blind, but this is a myth. All bat species can see, and some larger fruit bats have excellent vision. Many bats also use echolocation, but they use it in addition to their eyesight, not in place of it.
text_structure.r: To correct a common mistaken belief about bats
w: To explain how echolocation was discovered
To compare fruit bats with other mammals
To argue that bats should be protected
text_structure.e: The text opens by calling the belief a myth and then gives the facts. It never covers discovery, other mammals, or protection.

text_structure.s: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
text_structure.p: The town of Greenfield used to send all of its food scraps to a landfill. In 2019, the council started a compost program. Within two years, the amount of trash leaving the town had fallen by a third.
text_structure.r: It describes a problem, a response to it, and the result.
w: It compares two towns’ approaches to trash.
It presents an argument and then rejects it.
It lists the steps for making compost at home.
text_structure.e: Landfill waste is the problem, composting is the response, and less trash is the result. Only one town appears, and no instructions are given.

text_structure.s: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
text_structure.p: To make a paper airplane fly farther, start with a sharp center fold. Keep the nose heavy by folding it several times, and make sure both wings are the same size. Finally, throw it gently rather than hard.
text_structure.r: To give advice on improving a paper airplane’s flight
w: To explain the history of paper airplanes
To persuade readers to take up a new hobby
To describe how real airplanes are built
text_structure.e: Each sentence gives a practical tip for flying farther. There’s no history, argument for a hobby, or discussion of real aircraft.

text_structure.s: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?
text_structure.p: Octopuses are remarkable escape artists. In one aquarium, an octopus squeezed through a small drain and made its way to the sea. Because they have no bones, they can fit through almost any opening larger than their beak.
text_structure.r: It gives a specific example of the claim in the first sentence.
w: It challenges the claim in the first sentence.
It explains why octopuses have no bones.
It introduces a new topic unrelated to escaping.
text_structure.e: The drain story illustrates “escape artists.” It supports the first sentence, and the bones explanation comes only in the third sentence.

text_structure.s: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
text_structure.p: For decades, researchers assumed that the sounds of a coral reef were mere background noise. Marine ecologist Steve Simpson tested this idea by playing recordings of healthy reefs through underwater speakers on damaged reefs. Young fish arrived in far greater numbers at the sites with speakers than at silent sites, suggesting that fish use sound to find places to settle.
text_structure.r: To present a study showing that reef sounds influence where young fish settle
w: To argue that damaged reefs can be restored only with speakers
To explain how fish produce sounds on a healthy reef
To describe why researchers no longer study coral reefs
text_structure.e: The text sets up an assumption and reports an experiment that challenges it. It never claims speakers are the only way to restore reefs, and it doesn’t explain how fish make sounds.

text_structure.s: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
text_structure.p: The printing press is usually credited with spreading literacy across Europe. Yet historians point out that books remained too expensive for most people for more than a century after its invention. What changed reading habits more directly, they argue, was the later growth of cheap pamphlets and newspapers, which put printed words within ordinary budgets.
text_structure.r: It states a common view, raises a difficulty with it, and offers a different explanation.
w: It traces the invention of the printing press step by step.
It compares the prices of books in several European countries.
It defends a traditional view against a recent criticism.
text_structure.e: “Usually credited” is the common view, “Yet” raises the problem, and pamphlets are the alternative. The text challenges the traditional view rather than defending it.

text_structure.s: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
text_structure.p: The painter Jacob Lawrence told the story of the Great Migration in sixty small panels. Each panel uses only a few flat colors and simple shapes. This restraint might seem to limit what he could express, but it gives the series a steady rhythm, so that viewers feel the movement of a whole people rather than the drama of one individual.
text_structure.r: It anticipates a possible objection to Lawrence’s style before explaining the style’s effect.
w: It offers evidence that Lawrence’s panels were poorly received.
It shifts the discussion from Lawrence to other painters of his time.
It summarizes the historical causes of the Great Migration.
text_structure.e: “Might seem to limit” raises a doubt, and “but” turns to the benefit. No reception, other painters, or historical causes are mentioned.

text_structure.s: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
text_structure.p: Most people picture glaciers as slow and silent, but they can be surprisingly noisy. As ice shifts over bedrock, it cracks and groans. Near the ocean, trapped air bubbles burst as the ice melts, releasing a constant fizz. Scientists now use underwater microphones to measure these sounds and estimate how quickly a glacier is losing ice.
text_structure.r: To show that glacier sounds are both unexpected and scientifically useful
w: To warn that glaciers are dangerous to approach
To explain how air becomes trapped in glacial ice
To argue that microphones are better than satellites for studying ice
text_structure.e: The text moves from a surprising fact to its use in measurement. Satellites are never mentioned, and how air gets trapped isn’t explained.

text_structure.s: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
text_structure.p: Economists once treated the decision to save money as a straightforward calculation of future needs. Behavioral researchers complicated that picture by showing that people often behave inconsistently, resolving to save yet spending anyway. Rather than concluding that savers are simply irrational, however, Richard Thaler proposed changing the setting in which choices are made: when employees were automatically enrolled in retirement plans, and could opt out, participation rose sharply even though the available options had not changed at all.
text_structure.r: It outlines a traditional assumption, describes findings that challenge it, and presents an approach that responds to those findings.
w: It explains a theory, summarizes criticism of it, and concludes that the theory should be retained without revision.
It compares two retirement plans and recommends the one with the higher rate of return.
It describes an experiment, questions its methods, and calls for the experiment to be repeated.
text_structure.e: The text moves from the calculation view to inconsistent behavior to Thaler’s automatic enrollment. It doesn’t keep the old theory, compare two plans’ returns, or question any methods.

text_structure.s: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion, “a claim that says more about its authors than about the poems,” in the text as a whole?
text_structure.p: Nineteenth-century editors of Emily Dickinson’s work smoothed her irregular rhymes and replaced her dashes with conventional punctuation, insisting that readers could not otherwise follow her meaning, a claim that says more about its authors than about the poems. When scholars restored the original manuscripts in the 1950s, readers proved perfectly capable of following her, and the disruptions the editors had removed came to be seen as central to her achievement.
text_structure.r: It signals that the editors’ justification reflected their own assumptions rather than a real problem with the work.
w: It suggests that the editors were secretly the authors of some of Dickinson’s poems.
It concedes that Dickinson’s meaning was difficult for readers to follow.
It introduces evidence that the manuscripts of the poems were unreliable.
text_structure.e: The phrase casts doubt on the editors’ reason by pointing back at them, and the next sentence confirms readers had no such problem. “Authors” refers to those who made the claim, not writers of the poems, which is the trap in the first wrong choice.

text_structure.s: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
text_structure.p: Studies of animal cognition have long been shaped by what is convenient to measure. Because mirror tests rely on vision, for example, they favor species that navigate primarily by sight, and animals that fail the test have sometimes been described as lacking self-recognition. Dogs, which rely heavily on smell, ignore their reflections, yet in a recent experiment they spent more time investigating their own scent when it had been altered than when it had not. Such results suggest that the absence of evidence in one sensory channel may reflect the limits of the test rather than the limits of the animal.
text_structure.r: To argue that a common test may misjudge animals whose main senses differ from the ones it relies on
w: To show that dogs are more intelligent than other animals that have taken mirror tests
To explain the procedure researchers use to alter the scent of a dog
To claim that studies of animal cognition have not produced any useful results
text_structure.e: The final sentence states the point: failure on a vision-based test may reflect the test, not the animal. The text doesn’t rank dogs’ intelligence, and “not produced any useful results” goes much too far.

text_structure.s: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?
text_structure.p: The rise of the novel in eighteenth-century England is often attributed to a growing middle class with time to read. This account has an obvious appeal, but it struggles to explain why readers in other prosperous societies of the period did not embrace long prose fiction with the same enthusiasm. Literary historians have therefore begun to look beyond leisure and income, examining instead the spread of circulating libraries, which lowered the cost of borrowing books, and the social habits that made reading aloud a shared household activity.
text_structure.r: It identifies a weakness in the explanation presented in the first sentence, which motivates the approach described next.
w: It provides additional evidence for the explanation presented in the first sentence.
It rejects the idea that novels were widely read in eighteenth-century England.
It introduces the claim that reading aloud was more popular than private reading.
text_structure.e: “Struggles to explain” marks a weakness, and “therefore” in the next sentence shows it prompted a new approach. The sentence doesn’t deny that novels were read; it questions why.

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 that homework should be eliminated?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
Homework adds stress to students’ lives and takes time away from family and sleep. Schools should stop assigning it entirely.

Text 2
Small amounts of homework can help students practice skills and build good habits. The problem is too much homework, not homework itself. Schools should keep assignments short.
cross_text.r: By arguing that homework should be reduced rather than eliminated
w: By agreeing that all homework should end
By claiming that students need much more homework
By denying that students feel any stress
cross_text.e: Text 2 says the problem is “too much homework” and recommends short assignments, so it would favor reducing, not ending, homework.

cross_text.s: Which choice best describes a difference in how the authors of Text 1 and Text 2 view electric scooters?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
Electric scooters give city residents a cheap, clean way to travel short distances. They cut down on car trips and make it easier to reach bus and train stops.

Text 2
Electric scooters often clutter sidewalks and put pedestrians at risk. Many cities have seen injuries rise since rental scooters arrived.
cross_text.r: Text 1 focuses on their benefits, while Text 2 focuses on the problems they cause.
w: Text 1 says they are expensive, while Text 2 says they are cheap.
Text 1 discusses injuries, while Text 2 discusses train stops.
Both authors believe scooters should be banned immediately.
cross_text.e: Text 1 lists advantages and Text 2 lists harms. The other choices swap details or claim a ban neither text proposes.

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, what would the author of Text 2 most likely say about the idea in Text 1 that dinosaurs were slow, cold-blooded reptiles?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
For many years, scientists pictured dinosaurs as slow, cold-blooded reptiles that dragged their tails along the ground.

Text 2
Fossil trackways show almost no tail marks, and bone studies suggest many dinosaurs grew quickly, like birds. These findings point to active, warm-blooded animals.
cross_text.r: It is not supported by fossil evidence.
w: It is supported by the bone studies.
It applies to birds but not to dinosaurs.
It was never held by scientists.
cross_text.e: Text 2’s evidence points to active animals, which conflicts with the older picture. It doesn’t deny that scientists once believed it.

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the suggestion in Text 1?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
Libraries should remove their print reference books. Nearly all of that information can now be found online, and the shelf space could be used for study rooms.

Text 2
Not every library visitor has reliable internet access at home, and many older adults prefer print. Libraries serve people best when they offer information in more than one form.
cross_text.r: By pointing out that some library users still depend on print materials
w: By agreeing that print books are no longer useful
By suggesting that libraries need fewer study rooms
By arguing that online information is always inaccurate
cross_text.e: Text 2 stresses visitors without internet and those who prefer print. It never discusses study rooms or the accuracy of online sources.

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
A 2018 survey found that people who owned dogs reported better health than those who did not. The researchers concluded that owning a dog improves health, likely because dogs require daily walks.

Text 2
People who choose to adopt a dog may already be more active and financially stable than people who do not. Studies comparing dog owners with non-owners therefore cannot easily separate the effects of the dog from the traits of the people who own one.
cross_text.r: By cautioning that the health difference may reflect who chooses to own dogs rather than an effect of the dogs themselves
w: By arguing that dog owners actually report worse health than non-owners
By claiming that daily walks provide no health benefits
By recommending that more people adopt dogs to improve their health
cross_text.e: Text 2 raises a selection problem: owners may already differ from non-owners. It doesn’t dispute the survey’s results or say walking is useless.

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely view the approach described in Text 1?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
To protect rare seabirds on islands, conservationists often remove invasive rats. On many islands the bird populations have rebounded within a few years, making rat removal one of the most reliable tools in island conservation.

Text 2
Removing an invasive species can have unexpected effects. On one sub-Antarctic island, eliminating cats allowed rabbits to multiply, and the rabbits then stripped away much of the island’s vegetation. Managers must study how species interact before they act.
cross_text.r: As potentially useful but in need of careful study of each island’s species beforehand
w: As harmful because seabirds never benefit from the removal of rats
As unnecessary because invasive species rarely affect native birds
As more effective on sub-Antarctic islands than anywhere else
cross_text.e: Text 2 doesn’t oppose removal outright; it warns of side effects and says managers must study interactions first. The other choices overstate or invent claims.

cross_text.s: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
The Silk Road is often imagined as a single road along which merchants carried goods all the way from China to Rome.

Text 2
Archaeological records reveal a web of shifting local routes. Most traders traveled only short distances, passing goods along to others at regional markets. Few individuals, if any, made the entire journey.
cross_text.r: Text 2 offers evidence that corrects the popular image described in Text 1.
w: Text 2 provides an example that supports the image described in Text 1.
Text 2 explains why merchants preferred Rome to China.
Text 2 shows that the Silk Road did not carry any goods.
cross_text.e: Text 1 describes how the road is “imagined,” and Text 2 replaces that with a web of short routes. Goods still moved, so the last choice goes too far.

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, on which point would the authors of Text 1 and Text 2 most likely agree?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
Four-day workweeks have raised morale at many companies. In trials, employees reported less burnout, and most firms saw no decline in output. More employers should adopt the schedule.

Text 2
The early trials of four-day workweeks are encouraging, since workers do report feeling better. But most participating firms volunteered, and they may not represent the economy as a whole. Hospitals and factories, for example, may find the schedule much harder to adopt.
cross_text.r: Employees in the trials reported benefits from a four-day workweek.
w: Every employer should adopt a four-day workweek immediately.
The trials were limited to hospitals and factories.
Output declined at most firms in the trials.
cross_text.e: Both texts note better well-being among workers. Text 2 resists a universal adoption, and Text 1 says output held steady.

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the interpretation in Text 1?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
The stone circles of Neolithic Britain were, according to many archaeologists, primarily astronomical instruments. The precise alignment of several monuments with the solstices demonstrates that their builders were systematically tracking the sun, and it suggests that the sites functioned as a kind of calendar for an agricultural society.

Text 2
Alignments are easy to find if one looks for them: with enough stones and enough celestial events, some matches will occur by chance. Even where an alignment was intended, it need not imply calendrical record keeping. A monument oriented toward the midwinter sunset may have marked a single annual ceremony, with the alignment serving ritual purposes rather than practical timekeeping.
cross_text.r: By contending that even a genuine alignment would not establish that the monuments were used to keep a calendar
w: By denying that any Neolithic monument was built with the sun in mind
By arguing that the builders were more interested in the stars than in the sun
By asserting that Neolithic societies did not depend on agriculture
cross_text.e: Text 2 grants that an alignment may be intended but says it could be ritual, not timekeeping. “Denying that any” is too strong because of “Even where an alignment was intended.”

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 1 most likely respond to the point made in the final sentence of Text 2?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
Critics who judge a translation only by its fidelity to the original miss what translation is for. A translator’s first obligation is to produce a work that lives in the new language, and this may require departing from the original’s exact wording, its sentence structure, even its images, when these would strike new readers as stilted.

Text 2
Translators who treat smoothness as their highest goal risk erasing what makes a foreign text foreign. If every strange turn of phrase is converted into something familiar, readers learn nothing about how another culture thinks. A good translation should leave some strangeness in place, even at the cost of a little awkwardness.
cross_text.r: By maintaining that a translation that reads awkwardly fails in the translator’s primary duty, even if it preserves some strangeness
w: By agreeing that a translator’s highest duty is to preserve the foreign text’s exact wording
By arguing that foreign texts contain few phrases that seem strange to readers
By claiming that translators should stop translating images entirely
cross_text.e: Text 1 ranks a living work in the new language first, so it would reject accepting awkwardness. It explicitly allows departures from exact wording, which rules out the first wrong choice.

cross_text.s: Based on the texts, what would the author of Text 2 most likely say about the researchers’ conclusion in Text 1?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
In a laboratory study, participants who had just read literary fiction scored higher on a test of recognizing others’ emotions than participants who had read popular fiction or nonfiction. The researchers concluded that reading literary fiction immediately improves a person’s capacity to understand other people.

Text 2
Several teams have tried to reproduce the short-term effect of literary fiction on emotion recognition, with mixed results. What has held up better is a correlation: people who read a great deal of fiction over a lifetime tend to score higher on such tests. Whether reading builds this ability, however, or whether perceptive people simply enjoy fiction more, remains an open question.
cross_text.r: It is not well established, because the immediate effect has not been consistently reproduced.
w: It is confirmed by the correlation between lifetime reading and test scores.
It is incorrect, because fiction readers score lower on tests of emotion recognition.
It applies only to people who read popular fiction rather than literary fiction.
cross_text.e: Text 2 reports “mixed results” for the short-term effect. The correlation it describes is about lifetime reading, and it explicitly doesn’t prove cause, so it can’t confirm the immediate claim.

cross_text.s: Which choice best describes how the author of Text 2 would most likely regard the assumption underlying the policy in Text 1?
cross_text.p:
Text 1
The city’s plan to widen Route 9 rests on simple arithmetic. The road now carries more traffic than its two lanes can handle, and travel times have doubled in a decade. Adding two lanes will increase capacity by roughly 100 percent and restore the commute that residents once enjoyed.

Text 2
Transportation researchers have documented a pattern known as induced demand. When a road is widened, driving on it becomes temporarily easier, which draws drivers from other routes and other times of day and encourages new trips. In many metropolitan areas, traffic on expanded highways has returned to earlier levels of congestion within a few years.
cross_text.r: As flawed, because it treats the amount of traffic as fixed when added capacity tends to generate more driving
w: As sound, because adding lanes reliably reduces congestion for many decades
As irrelevant, because Route 9 is not a metropolitan highway
As outdated, because residents now commute less than they did a decade ago
cross_text.e: Text 1 assumes the same traffic spread over more lanes. Induced demand says more lanes bring more traffic, so that assumption is flawed. Text 2 says nothing about Route 9 specifically or about commuting declines.
